Chapter overview

Principles of the Self-Respect Movement examines the movement’s core programme of dignity, equality, caste abolition, rationalism, women’s autonomy, marriage reform, scientific temper, labour dignity and social liberation.

Dignity & equalityCaste & rationalismWomen & marriageEducation, labour & languageSocial and constitutional significance
Meaning, Scope and Purpose of Self-Respect

Self-respect is an egalitarian social principle that joins individual dignity with the removal of caste, gender, ritual and institutional domination.

Meaning of Self-Respect

Self-respect means recognition of one’s own:

  • Human dignity
  • Equality
  • Capacity to reason
  • Right to make personal decisions
  • Freedom from degrading customs
  • Right to live without social humiliation

In Tamil, the movement was commonly associated with expressions such as:

  • Suya Mariyathai
  • Thanmaanam

Self-respect was not treated as personal pride or arrogance.

It meant refusing to accept that any person was naturally:

  • Superior
  • Inferior
  • Pure
  • Polluting
  • Born to command
  • Born to serve
Self-Respect as a Social Principle

The movement argued that genuine self-respect was impossible when society was organised through:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • Untouchability
  • Patriarchy
  • Hereditary occupation
  • Priestly domination
  • Blind obedience
  • Unequal access to education
  • Social exclusion

An individual could not attain dignity merely through private confidence while continuing to accept institutions that degraded other human beings.

Collective Character

Self-respect therefore had two dimensions.

Individual Dimension

Every person should:

  • Think independently
  • Question authority
  • Choose a partner freely
  • Reject humiliating practices
  • Control their own life
Collective Dimension

Society should remove:

  • Caste barriers
  • Gender inequality
  • Ritual status
  • Social segregation
  • Hereditary privilege
  • Institutional discrimination
Central Objective

The movement sought to create a society in which human relationships were based on:

  • Equality
  • Reason
  • Mutual respect
  • Voluntary cooperation
  • Social justice

The Self-Respect Movement emerged in 1925 and placed opposition to caste hierarchy, patriarchy and religiously sanctioned inequality at the centre of its social programme.

Human Dignity, Individuality and Freedom from Submission

The movement treated dignity as inherent and encouraged independent judgement while rejecting mental submission to birth, custom or unjust authority.

Human Dignity

The movement treated dignity as an inherent human quality.

Dignity did not depend upon:

  • Caste
  • Family
  • Occupation
  • Wealth
  • Religious status
  • Gender
  • Ritual purity
  • Knowledge of sacred texts

No person needed permission from a religious or social superior to claim human worth.

Development of Individuality

The movement encouraged people to develop:

  • Independent judgement
  • Confidence
  • Courage to disagree
  • Capacity for self-government
  • Responsibility for personal choices

It opposed social training that demanded unquestioning obedience from:

  • Lower castes to dominant castes
  • Women to men
  • Labourers to hereditary elites
  • Laypersons to priests
  • Younger people to oppressive family authority
Freedom from Mental Slavery

Mental submission was considered as damaging as legal or economic oppression.

A person who believed that inferiority was fixed by:

  • Birth
  • Karma
  • Fate
  • Scripture
  • Divine punishment

might accept exploitation without resistance.

The movement therefore tried to remove the internal belief that inequality was natural.

Authority Must Be Justified

No institution was to be obeyed merely because it was:

  • Ancient
  • Religious
  • Traditional
  • Supported by custom
  • Practised by ancestors

Authority had to be examined according to:

  • Reason
  • Justice
  • Human welfare
  • Equality
Freedom and Responsibility

Individual freedom did not mean freedom to dominate another person.

It meant freedom exercised with recognition of:

  • Equal rights
  • Mutual consent
  • Social responsibility
  • Human dignity
Equality and Rejection of Birth-Based Hierarchy

Equality required rejection of superior and inferior birth and also corrective access for communities historically excluded from education, employment and public power.

Equality as the Foundation

Equality was the central organising principle of the Self-Respect Movement.

It opposed social divisions that assigned different rights according to birth.

The movement rejected the assumption that people were born into permanently unequal categories.

Rejection of Superior and Inferior Birth

Birth could not determine:

  • Intelligence
  • Character
  • Moral value
  • Occupation
  • Educational opportunity
  • Marriage rights
  • Political representation
  • Religious access
  • Social honour

The movement maintained that the idea of self-respect could not coexist with belief in superior and inferior castes.

Equality in Daily Life

Equality was not confined to legal declarations.

It had to be practised through:

  • Common access to schools
  • Common use of roads and public spaces
  • Equal seating
  • Inter-dining
  • Equal employment opportunity
  • Equal participation in public institutions
  • Freedom to choose occupations
  • Equal treatment of women
Equality of Status and Opportunity

The movement demanded more than formal equality.

Communities historically denied education and public employment required:

  • Representation
  • Educational access
  • Institutional protection
  • Removal of discriminatory barriers

This principle supported policies intended to correct inherited inequality.

Social Equality and Economic Equality

The movement’s discussions also recognised that social dignity could be weakened by extreme economic inequality.

A society divided between:

  • Owners and dependent labourers
  • Wealthy elites and impoverished workers
  • Educated groups and excluded communities

could not fully realise equality.

The movement’s public formulations linked the removal of caste and gender distinctions with broader social and economic equality.

Caste Abolition and Eradication of Untouchability

Caste was understood as a system governing marriage, occupation, residence and public access; the goal was abolition rather than limited accommodation.

Caste as a System

The movement did not treat caste merely as personal prejudice.

It understood caste as a system regulating:

  • Marriage
  • Food
  • Occupation
  • Residence
  • Education
  • Religious participation
  • Political influence
  • Social interaction
Abolition, Not Mere Reform

The objective was not simply to make caste relations kinder.

The movement called for removal of the structure that classified human beings by birth.

Limited Caste Reform
  • Reduces extreme cruelty
  • Permits selected access
  • Retains caste identities and hierarchy
Caste Abolition
  • Rejects birth-based rank
  • Removes hereditary social status
  • Encourages inter-caste relations
  • Establishes equal citizenship
Untouchability

Untouchability was condemned as:

  • Inhuman
  • Irrational
  • Socially degrading
  • A denial of common humanity

The movement opposed exclusion from:

  • Roads
  • Wells
  • Schools
  • Temples
  • Hotels
  • Public institutions
  • Residential areas
Caste Names and Suffixes

The use of caste titles in personal names was criticised because it publicly reproduced:

  • Hereditary identity
  • Social rank
  • Group separation

Removing caste suffixes was promoted as a symbolic step towards common human identity.

Hereditary Occupation

The movement rejected the belief that a person must follow the occupation of their ancestors.

Occupation should depend upon:

  • Ability
  • Training
  • Preference
  • Opportunity

It should not be imposed through caste.

Inter-Caste Marriage

Inter-caste marriage was regarded as one of the strongest practical challenges to caste because caste continuity depended heavily upon marriage within the group.

Limits of Non-Brahmin Unity

The movement’s anti-caste principle was broader than opposition to Brahmin dominance alone.

Replacing one dominant caste with another would not produce equality.

True self-respect required dignity for communities subjected to:

  • Untouchability
  • Landlessness
  • Occupational stigma
  • Social violence
Rationalism, Enquiry and Liberation of the Intellect

Rationalism liberated the intellect by making evidence, experience and human welfare the tests of inherited belief and social practice.

Meaning of Rationalism

Rationalism means examining beliefs through:

  • Evidence
  • Experience
  • Logical reasoning
  • Open discussion
  • Human consequences

A belief should not be accepted only because it was:

  • Ancient
  • Sacred
  • Popular
  • Supported by an authority
  • Followed by previous generations
Liberation of the Intellect

The Self-Respect Movement has been described as an intellectual-liberation movement because it encouraged people to free their thinking from inherited fear and obedience.

Intellectual liberation involved the right to:

  • Ask questions
  • Demand proof
  • Reject contradiction
  • Change one’s opinion
  • Criticise institutions
  • Discuss prohibited subjects
Reason and Social Reform

Reason was not promoted only as an abstract philosophy.

It was used to examine whether a custom:

  • Protected human dignity
  • Promoted equality
  • Caused suffering
  • Benefited a privileged group
  • Restricted women
  • Reinforced caste
Human Welfare as a Test

The movement evaluated social practices according to their effect on living people.

A practice causing:

  • Humiliation
  • Exclusion
  • Poverty
  • Fear
  • Gender oppression

could not be defended merely by describing it as traditional.

Freedom of Thought

Freedom of thought required freedom from punishment for questioning:

  • Scripture
  • Religious leaders
  • Caste rules
  • Family customs
  • Gender roles
  • Political leaders
Rationalism versus Education Alone

Formal education did not automatically produce rationalism.

An educated person might still support:

  • Untouchability
  • Gender inequality
  • Astrology-based discrimination
  • Birth-based status

Rationalism required continuous critical examination.

Opposition to Superstition, Fatalism and Irrational Customs

Superstition and fatalism were criticised when they created fear, hid human causes of suffering or protected social and economic exploitation.

Superstition

The movement criticised beliefs and practices accepted without adequate evidence.

Its criticism focused especially on customs that produced:

  • Fear
  • Financial exploitation
  • Social control
  • Gender discrimination
  • Caste inequality
Fatalism

Fatalism is the belief that present suffering is unavoidable because it has been predetermined by:

  • Fate
  • Karma
  • Previous birth
  • Divine will

The movement argued that fatalism discouraged people from changing unjust social conditions.

Social Effect of Karma-Based Explanations

When poverty, caste status or widowhood was presented as punishment for past actions, the social causes of suffering were hidden.

The movement instead directed attention towards:

  • Human institutions
  • Unequal power
  • Discrimination
  • Lack of education
  • Economic exploitation
Meaningless Ceremonies

Ceremonies were criticised when they:

  • Required unnecessary expenditure
  • Increased family debt
  • Gave control to hereditary specialists
  • Treated women as subordinate
  • Reinforced caste boundaries
  • Had no connection with human welfare
Fear as an Instrument of Control

Beliefs concerning:

  • Divine punishment
  • Ritual pollution
  • Horoscope incompatibility
  • Inauspicious times
  • Curses
  • Birth-based impurity

could be used to prevent individuals from exercising free choice.

Scientific Outlook

The alternative promoted by the movement was:

  • Observation
  • Evidence
  • Public reasoning
  • Medical knowledge
  • Secular education

Opposition to superstition was therefore connected to social equality rather than confined to disbelief in isolated customs.

Religion, Scriptural Authority and Hereditary Priesthood

The movement challenged scriptural claims and hereditary priesthood whenever religious authority governed civil rights, caste, marriage or gender relations.

Religion and Social Power

The movement examined religion not only as private belief but also as an institution influencing:

  • Caste
  • Marriage
  • Property
  • Women’s status
  • Education
  • Occupation
  • Public authority
Criticism of Scriptural Authority

Texts or interpretations supporting birth-based inequality were rejected.

The movement argued that no scripture should stand above:

  • Reason
  • Equality
  • Human dignity
  • Justice
Hereditary Priesthood

The principle of hereditary priesthood was criticised because it reserved religious authority for a birth-based group.

The criticism concerned:

  • Exclusive control of rituals
  • Claims of sacred superiority
  • Dependence upon priests
  • Ritual separation
  • Economic extraction
Priestless Ceremonies

The movement promoted ceremonies without a hereditary priest to demonstrate that:

  • Individuals could conduct their own social functions.
  • Marriage did not require priestly mediation.
  • Human consent was more important than ritual authority.
  • Community recognition could replace sacred hierarchy.
Religion as a Personal Matter

Private belief was distinguished from the use of religion to deny equal rights.

A belief could not legitimately justify:

  • Untouchability
  • Child marriage
  • Women’s subordination
  • Denial of education
  • Hereditary occupation
  • Public discrimination
Atheism and Social Criticism

Atheistic criticism became an important element of the movement’s propaganda.

However, the central social test was whether a belief or institution:

  • Preserved hierarchy
  • Restricted reason
  • Denied human equality

The complete development of Periyar’s atheistic and religious criticism belongs to Chapter 28.

Women’s Equality and Freedom from Patriarchy

Women were treated as autonomous individuals entitled to education, employment, property, bodily freedom and equal decision-making within family and public life.

Women as Equal Human Beings

The movement rejected the idea that women existed primarily as:

  • Daughters under fathers
  • Wives under husbands
  • Mothers serving families
  • Guardians of caste purity

Women were recognised as individuals with their own:

  • Intelligence
  • Preferences
  • Ambitions
  • Property interests
  • Political rights
  • Bodily autonomy
Equality in Education

Girls and women required equal access to:

  • Schooling
  • Higher education
  • Professional training
  • Public employment
  • Political knowledge

Education was necessary for economic independence and informed decision-making.

Economic Independence

Dependence upon male relatives could prevent women from escaping:

  • Abusive marriages
  • Forced marriages
  • Domestic control
  • Enforced widowhood

The movement therefore connected women’s freedom with:

  • Employment
  • Property rights
  • Equal wages
  • Education
Criticism of Chastity Standards

The movement opposed unequal moral standards under which:

  • Women’s sexuality was tightly controlled.
  • Men were permitted greater freedom.
  • Family honour was placed upon women alone.
  • Widows were punished for the death of husbands.

A moral rule could not be valid if it applied only to one gender.

Household Equality

Marriage was to be a partnership rather than a relationship of command and obedience.

This implied:

  • Shared decision-making
  • Mutual respect
  • Shared domestic responsibility
  • Equal dignity
  • Freedom from violence
Political Participation

Women participated in:

  • Conferences
  • Publications
  • Public speaking
  • Reform campaigns
  • Agitations

The movement’s gender programme included partner choice, widow remarriage, divorce rights and reproductive autonomy, making women’s equality central rather than incidental to its ideology.

Marriage Reform and the Principle of Free Consent

Marriage reform placed informed consent and equality above caste approval, horoscope, parental coercion, priesthood and expensive ritual.

Marriage as a Social Contract

The movement treated marriage primarily as an agreement between two individuals.

Its legitimacy should arise from:

  • Free consent
  • Mutual affection
  • Equal status
  • Public acknowledgement

It should not depend solely upon:

  • Priesthood
  • Horoscope
  • Caste permission
  • Expensive ritual
  • Parental coercion
  • Sacred-language recitation
Consent

Consent had to be:

  • Voluntary
  • Informed
  • Expressed by both partners
  • Free from force

Marriage arranged without the meaningful agreement of the woman was rejected.

Partner Choice

Adults should have the right to choose partners irrespective of:

  • Caste
  • Sub-caste
  • Widowhood
  • Family prestige
  • Horoscope
Opposition to Child Marriage

Child marriage was opposed because a child could not provide informed consent.

It also caused:

  • Interrupted education
  • Early pregnancy
  • Economic dependence
  • Premature widowhood
  • Loss of personal freedom
Opposition to Dowry and Ritual Expenditure

Marriage expenditure often created:

  • Debt
  • Financial pressure
  • Preference for sons
  • Treatment of daughters as burdens

Simple marriages were therefore promoted.

Marriage and Equality

A reformed marriage should not include rituals symbolising:

  • Female submission
  • Male ownership
  • Caste superiority
  • Priestly control

The central relationship was between the partners, not between their castes or ritual authorities.

Self-Respect Marriages: Form, Purpose and Legal Recognition

Self-Respect marriages provided a simple, consent-based social institution that began decades before statutory recognition under Tamil Nadu Section 7-A.

Meaning

A Self-Respect marriage is commonly known as:

  • Suyamariyathai marriage
  • Seerthiruththa marriage or reform marriage

It places mutual consent above priestly ritual.

Essential Features

Self-Respect marriages generally emphasised:

  • Consent of both partners
  • Public declaration
  • Equality
  • Absence of a hereditary priest
  • Simple ceremony
  • Use of an understandable language
  • Freedom from compulsory religious ritual
Possible Forms

The partners could express their marriage through:

  • Mutual declaration
  • Exchange of garlands
  • Exchange of rings
  • Tying of the thali where voluntarily chosen

No single religious ritual was treated as universally compulsory.

Social Purpose

Self-Respect marriages sought to:

  • Challenge priestly monopoly
  • Reduce expenditure
  • Weaken caste restrictions
  • Promote widow remarriage
  • Enable inter-caste unions
  • establish equality between partners
Early Practice

Self-Respect marriages were practised from the late 1920s.

Early forms sometimes removed the priest while retaining selected customary elements.

More radical ceremonies later excluded religious rituals and centred entirely on mutual declaration and social acknowledgement.

Legal Recognition

Tamil Nadu inserted Section 7-A into the Hindu Marriage Act through the Hindu Marriage (Tamil Nadu Amendment) Act, 1967.

Section 7-A recognises marriages between Hindus described as:

  • Suyamariyathai marriages
  • Seerthiruththa marriages
  • Other equivalent reform marriages

Such a marriage may be solemnised in the presence of relatives, friends or other persons through accepted forms including mutual declaration, exchange of garlands or rings, or tying of the thali.

Essential Distinction
Self-Respect Marriage Principle
  • Developed as a social-reform practice
  • Challenged caste, ritual and priestly authority
  • Emphasised consent and equality
Section 7-A
  • Statutory legal recognition
  • Introduced through the Tamil Nadu amendment
  • Applies within the legal framework specified by the provision

The social movement began decades before its marriages received explicit statutory recognition.

Widow Remarriage, Divorce and Reproductive Autonomy

Widow remarriage, divorce and reproductive autonomy extended women’s freedom beyond marriage into the right to leave, rebuild and control family decisions.

Enforced Widowhood

The movement opposed customs that punished women after the death of their husbands.

These included:

  • Denial of remarriage
  • Removal of ornaments
  • Restrictions on clothing
  • Social isolation
  • Exclusion from ceremonies
  • Treatment as inauspicious

A husband’s death could not reduce the widow’s human rights.

Widow Remarriage

Widows should possess the same right as widowers to:

  • Remarry
  • Choose a partner
  • Continue education
  • Work
  • Participate in public life

Widow remarriage was therefore both a women’s-rights principle and a challenge to caste patriarchy.

Divorce

Marriage was not to be treated as an unbreakable form of bondage.

The movement supported the right to leave a relationship involving:

  • Cruelty
  • Abandonment
  • Incompatibility
  • Denial of dignity
  • Absence of consent

The same moral and legal standards should apply to men and women.

Remarriage after Separation

A woman who divorced or separated from a husband should not be permanently stigmatised.

She retained the right to:

  • Remarry
  • Live independently
  • Rebuild her life
Reproductive Autonomy

The movement discussed women’s right to make decisions concerning:

  • Pregnancy
  • Number of children
  • Birth control
  • Maternal health

Compulsory motherhood was inconsistent with women’s freedom.

Family and Women’s Liberation

The movement did not assume that inequality existed only in public institutions.

The family itself could reproduce:

  • Male authority
  • Caste endogamy
  • Unequal labour
  • Property discrimination
  • Control of women’s sexuality

Social reform therefore had to enter domestic life.

Inter-Caste Marriage, Inter-Dining and Social Integration

Inter-caste marriage and inter-dining directly challenged endogamy, purity and pollution, but required wider structural equality to produce lasting integration.

Inter-Caste Marriage

Caste was reproduced through marriage within the same caste.

Inter-caste marriage directly challenged:

  • Endogamy
  • Hereditary identity
  • Caste purity
  • Family control
  • Segregated kinship
Inter-Religious Marriage

The movement also supported the freedom of adults to marry across religious boundaries.

The validity of a marriage should depend upon consent rather than religious uniformity.

Love Marriage

Love marriage was defended because it recognised the individual’s right to choose.

However, genuine choice required protection from:

  • Family violence
  • Caste councils
  • Social boycott
  • Economic coercion
Inter-Dining

Rules preventing people of different castes from eating together reinforced ideas of:

  • Pollution
  • Purity
  • Social distance

Inter-dining demonstrated practical equality.

Common Social Spaces

Social integration required common access to:

  • Schools
  • Public roads
  • Wells
  • Restaurants
  • Meeting halls
  • Transport
  • Workplaces
Limits of Symbolic Reform

A single inter-dining event could not by itself abolish caste.

Lasting change required:

  • Equal opportunity
  • Representation
  • Land and economic reform
  • Protection from violence
  • Continuous social interaction

Inter-caste marriage and inter-dining were therefore practical instruments within a broader anti-caste programme.

Education, Scientific Temper and Independent Thinking

Education was a means of emancipation only when it promoted evidence, independent thinking, scientific temper and equal institutional access.

Education as Liberation

Education enabled oppressed groups to:

  • Understand their rights
  • Challenge inherited status
  • Enter new occupations
  • Participate in administration
  • Read political publications
  • Question authority
Equal Educational Access

The movement supported expanded educational opportunities for:

  • Non-Brahmin communities
  • Adi Dravidas
  • Women
  • Rural populations
  • Economically disadvantaged groups
Education and Representation

When earlier exclusion had produced unequal access, equal treatment alone could preserve the existing imbalance.

Corrective measures were therefore justified to widen:

  • Admissions
  • Scholarships
  • Public employment
  • Institutional participation
Scientific Temper

Scientific temper involved:

  • Curiosity
  • Experiment
  • Evidence
  • Verification
  • Willingness to revise conclusions

It opposed explanations based exclusively on:

  • Fate
  • Horoscope
  • Ritual purity
  • Miracle
  • Hereditary intelligence
Education in the Mother Tongue

Accessible language was necessary for wider education.

Knowledge confined to an elite language could strengthen social monopoly.

Independent Thinking

Education should not merely train people to memorise authority.

It should help them:

  • Compare evidence
  • Identify contradictions
  • Analyse social power
  • Form independent conclusions
Education and Women

Women’s education was especially important because it strengthened:

  • Employment
  • Health awareness
  • Partner choice
  • Political participation
  • Control over family decisions
Economic Equality, Labour and Opposition to Exploitation

The movement connected caste and gender emancipation with dignity of labour, freedom of occupation, economic independence and opposition to exploitation.

Social and Economic Inequality

The movement recognised that caste oppression and economic exploitation often reinforced each other.

Communities assigned low social status were frequently concentrated in:

  • Poorly paid labour
  • Stigmatised occupations
  • Landless work
  • Domestic service
  • Agricultural dependence
Dignity of Labour

No honest occupation was inherently degrading.

The degradation arose when society:

  • Forced occupations by birth
  • Paid workers unequally
  • Treated manual labourers as inferior
  • Reserved prestigious employment for privileged groups
Freedom of Occupation

Every person should be able to choose and change occupations through:

  • Education
  • Training
  • Ability
  • Preference
Opposition to Hereditary Labour

The claim that children must continue their family occupation was rejected because it reproduced:

  • Caste
  • Poverty
  • Unequal education
  • Social immobility
Economic Independence and Women

Women required access to:

  • Employment
  • Property
  • Income
  • Professional training

Without economic independence, formal rights could remain ineffective.

Wealth and Social Power

Extreme concentration of wealth allowed privileged groups to influence:

  • Education
  • Politics
  • Publications
  • Public institutions

Economic democracy was therefore relevant to self-respect.

Socialism and the Movement

Socialist and labour ideas entered Self-Respect discussions, particularly through interaction with labour-oriented and left thinkers.

However, the movement’s entire economic history and Periyar’s changing political alliances belong mainly to Chapter 28.

Language, Culture and Recovery of Social Dignity

Tamil and understandable public language could recover dignity and democratise knowledge, but language pride without social equality remained inadequate.

Language and Power

Language could function as an instrument of social power when:

  • Administration used an inaccessible language.
  • Rituals were performed in a language people did not understand.
  • Classical status was used to claim cultural superiority.
  • Employment depended upon linguistic privilege.
Understandable Language

The movement supported the use of language understood by participants in:

  • Marriage declarations
  • Public meetings
  • Education
  • Political communication
  • Social ceremonies
Tamil and Social Dignity

Tamil cultural assertion was connected to:

  • Rejection of inferiority
  • Recovery of historical confidence
  • Wider public education
  • Opposition to exclusive Sanskritic authority
Language Is Not Enough

Tamil pride without caste abolition would not create self-respect.

A Tamil-speaking person could still practise:

  • Untouchability
  • Patriarchy
  • Caste violence
  • Hereditary inequality

Language dignity therefore had to be linked with social equality.

Cultural Reform

The movement did not accept every practice as valuable merely because it was Tamil or ancient.

Culture itself had to be judged through:

  • Reason
  • Equality
  • Human welfare
Chapter Boundary

The wider political principles of:

  • Linguistic rights
  • Anti-Hindi mobilisation
  • Regional identity
  • Federalism
  • State autonomy

belong mainly to Chapter 27.

Social Liberation before Political Liberation

Political independence was considered incomplete unless family, village, education, religion and employment were freed from caste, patriarchy and mental submission.

Political Freedom

Political freedom refers primarily to freedom from foreign rule and the establishment of representative government.

The movement argued that political independence alone would not automatically remove:

  • Caste
  • Untouchability
  • Male domination
  • Religious hierarchy
  • Unequal education
  • Hereditary privilege
Social Freedom

Social freedom meant the ability to live without:

  • Humiliation
  • Birth-based restrictions
  • Forced obedience
  • Gender subordination
  • Ritual exclusion
Political Independence without Equality

A transfer of political power could leave existing social elites in control.

Therefore, replacing foreign rulers with local rulers was insufficient if ordinary people remained subordinate in:

  • Family life
  • Village society
  • Education
  • Religion
  • Employment
Priority of Social Transformation

The movement gave priority to:

  • Changing social consciousness
  • Reforming marriage
  • Abolishing caste
  • Liberating women
  • Promoting rationalism
  • Establishing representation
Freedom Begins in Everyday Life

A person could not be considered fully free while being denied:

  • Choice of marriage
  • Equal education
  • Public access
  • Occupational mobility
  • Freedom of thought
Essential Distinction
Political Liberation
  • Change in government or sovereignty
  • Transfer of political power
  • Constitutional institutions
Self-Respect Liberation
  • Transformation of social relations
  • Removal of mental submission
  • Equality in family and society
  • Freedom from caste and patriarchy

The movement did not necessarily treat political and social freedom as mutually exclusive. It argued that political freedom would remain incomplete without social equality.

Organisation, Propaganda and Transformation of Daily Life

Conferences, publications and reform practices converted principles into daily acts such as priestless marriages, removal of caste suffixes and women’s public participation.

Reform through Practice

The movement did not confine itself to speeches or theoretical resolutions.

Its principles were practised through:

  • Self-Respect marriages
  • Widow remarriages
  • Inter-caste dining
  • Removal of caste titles
  • Women’s conferences
  • Public debates
  • Rationalist campaigns
Conferences

Conferences enabled participants to discuss:

  • Caste abolition
  • Women’s rights
  • Marriage reform
  • Education
  • Religion
  • Representation
  • Economic inequality

They also created networks among local activists.

Publications

Newspapers and journals carried:

  • Speeches
  • Editorials
  • Debates
  • Reports of reform marriages
  • Criticism of customs
  • Women’s writing
  • International reform ideas

Kudi Arasu, launched in Erode in May 1925, became a major vehicle for Self-Respect propaganda. The English journal Revolt later carried related ideas to English-reading audiences.

Accessible Communication

The movement used:

  • Simple Tamil
  • Satire
  • Questions
  • Public controversy
  • Short slogans
  • Illustrations
  • Dramatic speeches

This allowed social criticism to reach beyond universities and elite organisations.

Women as Agents

Women were not presented only as beneficiaries.

They participated as:

  • Speakers
  • Writers
  • Organisers
  • Protesters
  • Conference leaders
Personal Conduct as Politics

Acts such as:

  • Removing a caste suffix
  • Conducting a priestless marriage
  • Supporting widow remarriage
  • Rejecting untouchability
  • Educating daughters

were treated as political because they challenged structures of power.

Non-Electoral Emphasis

The movement initially concentrated primarily on transforming society rather than winning government office.

Its social programme later influenced several political organisations, but those developments belong to Chapters 25 and 27–29.

Democratic, Humanist and Constitutional Significance

The principles anticipated democratic, humanist and constitutional commitments while requiring a distinction between proclaimed equality and incomplete social achievement.

Humanist Character

The movement placed the human being above:

  • Ritual
  • Scripture
  • Caste
  • Tradition
  • Hereditary status

Human welfare was the central test of institutions.

Democratic Character

Democracy required more than elections.

It required equality within:

  • Family
  • School
  • Workplace
  • Public space
  • Religious institutions
  • Political organisations
Equality before Law

The movement’s principles anticipated or reinforced constitutional values such as:

  • Equality
  • Non-discrimination
  • Abolition of untouchability
  • Personal liberty
  • Freedom of expression
  • Educational opportunity
Social Justice

Social justice required correction of historically accumulated disadvantage.

It therefore included:

  • Representation
  • Educational access
  • Protection of oppressed communities
  • Removal of institutional barriers
Secular Significance

The movement opposed the use of religious authority to determine civil rights.

Marriage, education and public employment were to be governed by:

  • Consent
  • Equality
  • Civil law
  • Public reason
Feminist Significance

Its women’s-rights programme addressed:

  • Marriage choice
  • Widowhood
  • Divorce
  • Education
  • Employment
  • Reproductive decisions
  • Unequal sexual morality
Continuing Legal Significance

Section 7-A remains an important legal expression of the Self-Respect marriage principle in Tamil Nadu.

Courts have continued to interpret the requirements and validity of marriages solemnised under the provision.

Balanced Assessment

The movement transformed public discussion concerning:

  • Caste
  • Gender
  • Religion
  • Marriage
  • Language
  • Representation

However, ideological commitment did not automatically eliminate:

  • Caste violence
  • Patriarchy
  • Economic inequality
  • Unequal representation
  • Discrimination within non-Brahmin communities

The distinction between proclaimed principles and complete social achievement must be maintained.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates principles, practices, chronology, legal distinctions and the high-yield contrasts most likely to appear in TNPSC examinations.

Core Principles
  • Human dignity
  • Equality
  • Caste abolition
  • Eradication of untouchability
  • Rationalism
  • Freedom of thought
  • Opposition to superstition
  • Rejection of hereditary priesthood
  • Women’s equality
  • Marriage by free consent
  • Widow remarriage
  • Divorce rights
  • Inter-caste marriage
  • Education
  • Scientific temper
  • Dignity of labour
  • Economic independence
  • Social liberation
Essential Chronology
  • 1925 — Self-Respect Movement emerged under Periyar’s leadership
  • 2 May 1925 — Kudi Arasu began publication at Erode
  • Late 1920s — Self-Respect marriages became an important movement practice
  • 1928 — Revolt began carrying movement ideas in English
  • 1929 — Major early Self-Respect conference phase
  • 1930s — Expansion of women’s participation, marriage reform and rationalist propaganda
  • 1944 — Justice Party transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam; Self-Respect principles became central to DK
  • 1967 — Tamil Nadu legislation introduced legal recognition for Self-Respect and reform marriages
  • 17 January 1968 — Presidential assent to the Tamil Nadu marriage amendment
  • 20 January 1968 — Amendment published following assent
Principle–Meaning Associations
  • Self-respect — refusal to accept humiliation
  • Equality — rejection of superior and inferior birth
  • Rationalism — examination through reason and evidence
  • Caste abolition — removal of birth-based status
  • Women’s liberation — equality in family and public life
  • Self-Respect marriage — marriage based on consent without compulsory priestly ritual
  • Social liberation — freedom from caste, patriarchy and mental submission
  • Scientific temper — willingness to question, verify and revise
  • Dignity of labour — no occupation is inferior by nature
  • Representation — corrective access for historically excluded communities
Practice–Purpose Associations
  • Removing caste suffixes — weaken public reproduction of caste identity
  • Inter-dining — challenge purity and pollution
  • Inter-caste marriage — challenge caste endogamy
  • Widow remarriage — oppose enforced widowhood
  • Priestless marriage — reject hereditary ritual control
  • Simple ceremony — reduce expenditure and debt
  • Women’s education — strengthen independence
  • Rationalist publication — spread critical thinking
  • Mother-tongue communication — democratise knowledge
  • Occupational choice — reject hereditary labour
High-Yield Distinctions
Self-Respect versus Personal Pride

Self-Respect

  • Recognition of equal human dignity
  • Opposes domination
  • Includes respect for others

Personal Pride

  • May concern individual status
  • Can exist without commitment to equality
  • May become arrogance

Self-respect is an egalitarian social principle, not personal vanity.

Caste Reform versus Caste Abolition

Caste reform

  • Reduces harsh practices
  • May retain caste identity
  • May retain endogamy

Caste abolition

  • Rejects birth-based hierarchy
  • Challenges endogamy
  • Seeks common human equality
Formal Equality versus Social Justice

Formal equality

  • Same rule for everyone
  • Does not necessarily correct previous exclusion

Social justice

  • Recognises historical disadvantage
  • Supports representation and corrective opportunity
Rationalism versus Mere Education

Rationalism

  • Questions authority
  • Examines evidence
  • Changes conclusions when required

Mere education

  • May produce literacy or qualifications
  • Does not automatically remove caste or superstition
Religious Belief versus Religious Domination

Religious belief

  • Personal matter of conscience

Religious domination

  • Uses belief to deny civil rights
  • Enforces hierarchy through public institutions

The movement’s central objection was to authority that produced inequality and prevented reason.

Traditional Marriage versus Self-Respect Marriage

Traditional ritual-centred marriage

  • May depend on priest and prescribed ceremony
  • Often shaped by caste endogamy
  • May use a language not understood by the partners

Self-Respect marriage

  • Based on mutual consent
  • Does not require hereditary priesthood
  • Uses public declaration or simple accepted forms
  • Promotes equality and reform
Self-Respect Marriage versus Civil Marriage

Self-Respect marriage

  • Originated as a social-reform practice
  • Later received recognition under Section 7-A in Tamil Nadu for marriages within its statutory scope

Civil marriage

  • Conducted under civil marriage legislation
  • Governed by its own statutory procedure

They should not be treated as legally identical.

Widow Remarriage versus Enforced Widowhood

Widow remarriage

  • Recognises continuing personal freedom
  • Applies equal standards to widows and widowers

Enforced widowhood

  • Restricts remarriage
  • Imposes clothing and social restrictions
  • Treats the widow as inauspicious
Political Freedom versus Social Freedom

Political freedom

  • Change in rulers
  • Representative government
  • Sovereignty

Social freedom

  • Caste equality
  • Women’s autonomy
  • Freedom of thought
  • Dignity in everyday life

The movement argued that political freedom was incomplete without social freedom.

Anti-Brahminism versus Anti-Brahmin

Criticism of Brahminism

  • Criticism of hereditary hierarchy
  • Opposition to ideological and institutional dominance

Hostility towards individuals by birth

  • Reproduces birth-based judgement
  • Conflicts with universal equality

The ideological target was a system of hierarchy, not the replacement of one birth-based hatred with another.

Women’s Welfare versus Women’s Liberation

Women’s welfare

  • Offers protection or assistance
  • May retain male guardianship

Women’s liberation

  • Recognises agency
  • Supports education, property, employment, consent and divorce
  • Treats women as equal individuals
Symbolic Reform versus Structural Reform

Symbolic reform

  • Removes a title or performs a single public act

Structural reform

  • Changes access to education, employment, property and power

Both may be useful, but symbolic acts alone cannot end institutional inequality.

Exam Traps
  • The Self-Respect Movement began in 1925.
  • Self-respect does not mean arrogance or individual vanity.
  • Equality, rationalism, caste abolition and women’s freedom are interconnected principles.
  • The movement sought caste abolition, not merely limited caste reform.
  • Opposition to Brahminism refers to opposition to hereditary ideological dominance; it should not be reduced to hatred of individuals.
  • The movement rejected hereditary priesthood and compulsory priestly mediation.
  • Rationalism means examination through reason and evidence.
  • Formal education alone does not necessarily produce rationalism.
  • Self-Respect marriages emphasise consent, equality and absence of compulsory priestly ritual.
  • Self-Respect marriages existed before their statutory recognition.
  • Section 7-A was inserted through the Tamil Nadu amendment to the Hindu Marriage Act.
  • Exchange of garlands, exchange of rings, mutual declaration or tying of the thali may satisfy the prescribed form; every element is not simultaneously compulsory.
  • The thali is not the sole universal requirement under Section 7-A.
  • Self-Respect marriage and marriage under the Special Marriage Act are not identical legal categories.
  • Widow remarriage was treated as a right, not an act of charity.
  • Women’s liberation included education, employment, consent, divorce and reproductive autonomy.
  • Inter-caste marriage challenged caste endogamy.
  • Inter-dining challenged notions of purity and pollution.
  • The movement opposed hereditary occupation.
  • Dignity of labour does not mean acceptance of caste-imposed labour.
  • Tamil cultural dignity was linked with social equality.
  • Tamil pride without caste abolition was considered insufficient.
  • Political independence without social equality was regarded as incomplete.
  • The movement sought transformation of family and everyday life, not merely governmental change.
  • Complete contributions of Periyar belong to Chapter 28.
  • Broader principles of the Dravidian Movement belong to Chapter 27.
  • Complete contributions of Anna belong to Chapter 29.
